blocks.text: A recursive program can be short enough to fit on a postcard and still explore more work than a machine can finish. The useful question is not whether the function calls itself. It is what becomes smaller, what the current call assumes, what remains true while a choice is active, and how the caller’s state is restored afterward. Those questions connect the correctness discipline of Chapter 1 to the structures and algorithms already built.

topics.title: 17.1 Designing Recursive Solutions
topics.summary: A recursive function needs a well-defined smaller problem and a stopping condition. The call stack remembers work that must resume after a child call completes. Recursion does not eliminate state; it gives that state a structured lifetime.

topics.title: 17.1.1 Defining Base Cases
topics.summary: A base case handles an input that no longer needs decomposition. In the queens problem, reaching row n means every row has a valid queen placement, so count one solution and return. The empty board also has one valid empty placement. This convention makes the combinatorial result for n=0 explicit rather than treating it as an accidental loop outcome.

blocks.text: A base case describes a state whose answer is available without making another recursive call. It should follow from the problem’s meaning rather than from a desire to stop the debugger. For a sum of an empty sequence, the result is zero. For counting arrangements after every row has received a valid queen, the result contributed by that arrangement is one. These are different empty-state meanings, and choosing the wrong identity can corrupt every larger result.

topics.title: 17.1.2 Reducing Problems Recursively
topics.summary: At row r, the smaller problem is to place queens in rows r+1 through n-1 after selecting a legal column for r. The number of unfilled rows decreases by one on every recursive call, so depth is at most n. This proves termination for the finite, bounded board even though the number of branches may be large.

blocks.text: The partial-placement invariant is: every earlier row has exactly one queen, no used column repeats, and neither diagonal family contains a conflict. The function does not need to recheck every pair of earlier queens if it maintains occupancy arrays that encode those facts.

blocks.text: Recursive decomposition should match the information passed down. Here the mutable occupancy arrays represent the current path, while the row number identifies progress. A function that copied the entire board at every branch would use a different memory and movement strategy. Neither style is inherently correct merely because it uses recursion; both must preserve the same legal-placement invariant.

blocks.text: Termination follows from a measure that decreases in a well-founded domain. Here that measure is the number of unassigned rows, n - row. A recursive call advances from row to row + 1, reducing the measure by one. Because calls begin at zero and stop at n, a chain contains at most n placements. This argument bounds recursion depth; it does not bound the number of different chains cheaply.

This is why a recursion that has a convincing termination argument can still be unsuitable for unrestricted input. The supplied n <= 12 teaching limit bounds the exercise, while the mathematical argument explains its structure.

It also explains why the recursive function does not need a second loop to choose a row: the row order has already been fixed by the decomposition. Each level chooses only a column for its own row.

blocks.text: Some recursive algorithms shrink by halving rather than subtracting one. Binary search reduces an interval, merge sort reduces segment lengths, and a tree traversal moves to proper subtrees. The relevant measure must match the representation. In a graph with cycles, moving to a neighbor does not necessarily reduce anything; a visited policy or a bounded search state is required.

topics.title: 17.2 Exploring Search Spaces with Backtracking
topics.summary: Backtracking explores a decision tree with a repeated pattern: choose, record, recurse, undo. The undo step makes sibling branches independent. Without it, a failed or completed branch contaminates later choices and silently removes valid solutions.

Clearing a bit that belonged to an earlier queen would corrupt the path, which is why “record first, validate later” is not equivalent.

The early empty-board return avoids computing an inappropriate diagonal size for n == 0.

The invariant is that these arrays describe exactly the placements made by the active ancestor calls. They do not describe every placement ever visited during the search.

blocks.text: Cleanup during ordinary return is not automatically cleanup during every failure. The present recursive body performs bounded marking and counting without a user callback. Adding a callback that may throw, a cancellation exception, or another fallible operation between marking and unmarking requires deliberate restoration. A scope-bound undo object can preserve the invariant during unwinding. Alternatively, redesign the state so each recursive call receives its own independent copy and accept the copying cost. Neither choice should be hidden behind the word “recursive.”

paragraphs: At row r, try each column c. A column occupancy bit rejects a reused column. One diagonal index is r+c; the other is r+n-1-c. For n>0, both lie between zero and 2n-2, so arrays of length 2n-1 are sufficient. The early n=0 return avoids unsigned underflow when computing that length.

For a legal choice, set its column and both diagonal bits, recurse to the next row, and clear those same three bits on return. The code relies on the legal-choice test to ensure those bits were previously false. Clearing a bit that belonged to an earlier queen would corrupt the path, which is why “record first, validate later” is not equivalent.

If a future extension performs throwing work after setting the bits, ordinary explicit cleanup after the recursive call would be skipped during unwinding. A scope guard or copied immutable state can provide rollback in that stronger model. The current bounded counter performs no dynamic allocation within the search after its arrays and callable are established, keeping the normal choose/undo mechanism easy to inspect.

Backtracking installs a tentative choice, explores the consequences, and removes that choice before considering the next alternative. The undo step is part of correctness. A board that retains a column mark from a completed sibling branch will reject valid future placements even though no real queen occupies that column in the current branch.

For the queens example, column[c] records whether an earlier row uses column c. The two diagonal arrays record row + c and row + n - 1 - c. Each index identifies one family of parallel diagonals. With 0 <= row,c < n, both expressions are between zero and 2*n - 2, which fits arrays of length 2*n - 1. The early empty-board return avoids computing an inappropriate diagonal size for n == 0.

Before placing a queen, all three marks must be false. The algorithm sets them true together, calls the next row, then sets them false together. The invariant is that these arrays describe exactly the placements made by the active ancestor calls. They do not describe every placement ever visited during the search.

The supplied program counts solutions but does not store each board. A sequence of selected columns could be added for visualization. Push a column before descending and remove it afterward, keeping its length equal to the current depth. Storing every complete solution changes the output-size and memory contract even when the search order stays the same.

Cleanup during ordinary return is not automatically cleanup during every failure. The present recursive body performs bounded marking and counting without a user callback. Adding a callback that may throw, a cancellation exception, or another fallible operation between marking and unmarking requires deliberate restoration. A scope-bound undo object can preserve the invariant during unwinding. Alternatively, redesign the state so each recursive call receives its own independent copy and accept the copying cost. Neither choice should be hidden behind the word “recursive.”

topics.title: 17.2.2 Pruning Impossible Solutions
topics.summary: Pruning rejects partial choices that cannot be extended to a legal solution under the current constraints. A column conflict already violates the final requirement, so exploring descendants cannot repair it. Rejecting that branch is therefore safe. A heuristic such as “this column looks unlikely” would need a different justification before it could discard solutions.

blocks.text: Pruning rejects a partial candidate when no completion of that candidate can satisfy the requirement. In the queens problem, an occupied column or diagonal proves that the proposed queen already conflicts with an earlier queen. Adding more queens cannot repair that conflict while earlier choices remain fixed. Skipping the branch is therefore sound.

blocks.text: A heuristic is different. Trying central columns first may change the order in which solutions are found, but it does not prove that other columns are impossible. A complete counting algorithm must still explore all legal alternatives unless a justified symmetry or equivalence rule accounts for the omitted work. Do not label an attractive guess as a correctness-preserving prune.

blocks.text: Separate soundness from completeness. Soundness says every counted board is valid. The marks enforce this locally, and the base case requires all rows to be assigned. Completeness says every valid board is eventually counted. Fixed row order plus iteration over every legal column supports that claim: the next column of any valid board is one of the alternatives considered at that level. Because each board has exactly one column choice per row, that construction also explains why it is counted once.

blocks.text: Symmetry reduction can be valuable, but its counting rule needs care. Reflecting a board can pair solutions, while some structures may map to themselves under a symmetry. A naive multiplication factor can overcount or undercount. Keep the straightforward reference search available before adding a symmetry-aware optimization, and compare exact counts for small boards where both are practical.

blocks.text: Pruning effectiveness depends on the instance and on the state representation. Testing all earlier placements for conflict would still be correct but would add work to each candidate. The three mark arrays summarize the same relevant information for constant-time conflict checks. That is a representation improvement separate from the combinatorial benefit of pruning entire branches.

topics.summary: Trace the first few calls for a four-row board on paper. Begin with no marks. Choose a legal column in row zero, record the affected column and diagonal indices, and move to row one. When no legal column remains, return to the caller and erase exactly the caller’s most recent choice. Do not erase an ancestor’s marks or leave a sibling’s marks behind.

Check the returned columns for uniqueness and pairwise diagonal separation independently of the search’s own occupancy arrays.
Engineering takeaway. Every recursive branch needs a progress measure, and every tentative mutation needs a defined restoration path.

topics.title: Review and solution reasoning
topics.summary: The recursion terminates because the number of unassigned rows decreases, not because the machine has a finite stack. Counting the empty arrangement as one follows the stated combinatorial convention. A conflicting partial placement can be pruned because retaining it cannot lead to a valid completion. Changing the order of legal alternatives alone does not change the solution set.
